title: GPS — Global Positioning System
notes: **Principle:** a GPS receiver calculates its 3D position (latitude, longitude, altitude) by measuring the time delay of radio signals from at least four satellites whose positions are known precisely.

**Satellite constellation:** 24+ operational satellites orbit at about $20,\!200\,\text{km}$ altitude (MEO) in six orbital planes inclined $55^\circ$ to the equator. This ensures at least four satellites are visible from any point on Earth at any time.
**Orbital parameters:** altitude $\approx 20,\!200\,\text{km}$, orbital period $\approx 12$ hours (sidereal time), velocity $\approx 3.87\,\text{km/s}$. Two complete orbits per sidereal day.
**Distance measurement:** distance = speed of light $\times$ time delay. A timing error of just $1\,\text{ns}$ causes a position error of about $0.3\,\text{m}$ along the line of sight.

**Relativistic corrections:** special relativity predicts clocks on satellites run slower by $\Delta f/f = -v^2/2c^2 \approx -0.84 \times 10^{-9}$ (about $-7.2\,\mu\text{s/day}$) due to their orbital speed. General relativity predicts they run faster by $\Delta f/f = \Delta U/c^2 \approx +5.45 \times 10^{-10}$ (about $+45.8\,\mu\text{s/day}$) due to weaker gravity. Net effect: satellite clocks gain $+38.7\,\mu\text{s/day}$, which must be corrected or GPS would accumulate errors of about $10\,\text{km}$ per day.

**Four satellites needed:** three give position in 3D space ($x, y, z$). The fourth is needed to solve for the receiver clock offset, since the receiver's inexpensive clock is not synchronized with satellite atomic clocks.
**Pseudo-range:** the measured distance to each satellite includes a clock bias: $\rho = r + c\delta t$. Four equations with four unknowns ($x, y, z, \delta t$) solve the problem.

**C/A code and P code:** the coarse acquisition (C/A) code on L1 frequency ($1575.42\,\text{MHz}$) provides $\approx 3\text{--}5\,\text{m}$ accuracy. The precision (P) code on L1 and L2 ($1227.60\,\text{MHz}$) provides $\approx 1\,\text{cm}$ accuracy for military users.
**Dilution of precision (DOP):** the geometry of visible satellites affects accuracy. Good DOP (well-spread satellites) gives better accuracy; poor DOP (satellites clustered) degrades accuracy.
**Other GNSS systems:** GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China), QZSS (Japan), IRNSS/NavIC (India). All use similar principles at different frequencies.

**Message structure:** each GPS satellite broadcasts a navigation message at $50\,\text{bps}$ containing ephemeris data (precise orbit), almanac (coarse orbit for all satellites), clock corrections, and health status.

**Receiver types:** consumer GPS receivers typically achieve $3\text{--}10\,\text{m}$ accuracy. Differential GPS (DGPS) using ground reference stations can achieve $1\text{--}3\,\text{m}$. Real-time kinematic (RTK) GPS can achieve centimeter-level accuracy.
**Aiding techniques:** Assisted GPS (A-GPS) uses cellular networks to provide satellite almanac and approximate position, enabling faster time-to-first-fix (TTFF) in mobile phones.
confusion: GPS satellites do NOT stay directly above fixed points — they orbit Earth. The receiver accounts for satellite motion using ephemeris data broadcast in the navigation message.

The $+38.7\,\mu\text{s/day}$ relativistic correction is NOT negligible — without it, GPS would be off by $10\,\text{km/day}$, making it completely useless. This is one of the most practical validations of relativity.

Four satellites are needed because of the receiver's unknown clock bias, not just for 3D positioning. A wristwatch cannot measure time precisely enough; the fourth satellite provides the time reference.
GPS altitude is measured relative to the WGS84 ellipsoid (a mathematical model of Earth's shape), not sea level. The difference between the ellipsoid and actual geoid can be $\pm 100\,\text{m}$.
GPS is not the only satellite navigation system — GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou provide global coverage, while regional systems like NavIC serve specific countries.
practice: A GPS satellite at altitude $20,\!200\,\text{km}$ broadcasts a signal. The receiver measures a time delay of $67.3\,\text{ms}$. What is the approximate distance? Solution: $d = c \times \Delta t = (3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s})(67.3 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}) = 2.02 \times 10^7\,\text{m} = 20,\!200\,\text{km}$. The delay matches the orbital altitude (two-way travel would be double).

If the relativistic correction for GPS satellites were NOT applied, how much error would accumulate in one day? Solution: Clock gains $+38.7\,\mu\text{s/day}$. Distance error = $c \times \Delta t = (3 \times 10^8)(38.7 \times 10^{-6}) = 11.6\,\text{km/day}$. In a year, the error would be over $4,\!000\,\text{km}$ — larger than Earth.

Calculate the orbital period of a GPS satellite. $r = R_E + h = 6378 + 20,\!200 = 26,\!578\,\text{km} = 2.658 \times 10^7\,\text{m}$. Solution: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM} = 2\pi\sqrt{(2.658 \times 10^7)^3/(3.986 \times 10^{14})} = 2\pi \times 46,\!170\,\text{s} \approx 43,\!000\,\text{s} \approx 11\,\text{h}\,58\,\text{min}$, close to 12 hours.

Three GPS satellites give ranges $\rho_1 = 22,\!000\,\text{km}$, $\rho_2 = 23,\!500\,\text{km}$, $\rho_3 = 21,\!800\,\text{km}$. The receiver's clock is slow by $10\,\text{ns}$. What is the true range to satellite 1? Solution: $\rho_1 = r_1 + c\delta t = r_1 + (3 \times 10^8)(10 \times 10^{-9}) = r_1 + 3\,\text{m}$. True range $r_1 = 22,\!000 - 3 = 21,\!999.997\,\text{km}$. The clock error of just $10\,\text{ns}$ creates a $3\,\text{m}$ range error.

What is the orbital velocity of a GPS satellite? $r = 26,\!578\,\text{km}$. Solution: $v = \sqrt{GM/r} = \sqrt{3.986 \times 10^{14}/2.658 \times 10^7} = \sqrt{1.50 \times 10^7} = 3873\,\text{m/s} = 3.87\,\text{km/s}$.
universalFacts: GPS is one of the most important practical applications of Einstein's theories of relativity — special and general relativity are both essential corrections that make GPS work.
GPS satellites carry atomic clocks (rubidium or cesium) accurate to about 1 nanosecond per day. Even this tiny drift must be corrected by ground control stations every day.
Every GPS satellite broadcasts its own ephemeris (orbital parameters) and the almanac (coarse data for all satellites), allowing the receiver to compute the satellite's position at any time.
GPS signals are incredibly weak (about as strong as a $50\,\text{W}$ light bulb seen from $20,\!200\,\text{km}$) — they can be blocked by buildings, trees, or intentionally jammed.
India's NavIC (IRNSS) system provides positioning services over India and the surrounding region with 7 satellites, reducing dependence on foreign GPS systems.
The first GPS satellite was launched in 1978, and the system achieved full operational capability in 1995. Today, over 4 billion people use GPS-enabled devices worldwide.
GPS accuracy has improved significantly over time — Selective Availability (intentional degradation) was turned off in 2000, and modern receivers can achieve sub-meter accuracy without augmentation.
